result.explanation: The intent raises C3’s RAM floor to 4.5 GB and C2’s RAM floor to 5 GB.  C3 already satisfies its new requirement on N6 (CPU 4.28 vCPU, RAM 4.5 GB).  C2, however, cannot stay on N4 because that node would then have only 3.83 GB of free RAM, below the 5 GB floor.  Moving C2 to N6 frees N4 for C4 and gives C2 a node with ample resources (N6 has 16 vCPU and 35 GB RAM; after adding C2 the node still has 11.7 vCPU and 30.5 GB RAM available).  No other services need to move, so the minimal‑move solution is to relocate only C2 to N6.

The intent requires C4 to have at least 4 vCPU and every service in the recognition chain (C1→C2→C3→C5) to have at least 4 vCPU.  C1 and C5 are fixed, so only C2 and C4 can move.

• C2 currently on N4 uses 3.22 vCPU.  Moving it to N6 frees 3.22 vCPU on N4, giving N4 enough headroom for C4 to reach the 4 vCPU floor.
• C4 on N4 needs 0.64 vCPU more.  After C2 leaves, N4 has 2.42 vCPU free, which is enough for C4 to stay on N4.  However, to satisfy the 4 vCPU requirement for C4 itself, we move C4 to N6, where the remaining capacity is ample.
• N6 has 16 vCPU and 35 GB RAM.  After moving C2 (3.22 vCPU, 2.17 GB) and C4 (3.36 vCPU, 3.0 GB) alongside the existing C3 (4.28 vCPU, 2.95 GB), the total usage is 11.86 vCPU and 8.12 GB, well within limits.

Thus moving C2 and C4 to N6 satisfies all new CPU thresholds while keeping the fixed services unchanged. No other placement with fewer moves can meet the requirements.

All current service placements satisfy the new latency constraints. For the Object Recognition Flow (C1→C2→C3→C5) the total service processing time is about 0.28 ms and the propagation delays along N12→N4 (10.3 ms), N4→N6 (5.0 ms) and N6→N8 (7.9 ms) add up to 23.2 ms, giving a total of ~23.5 ms, well below the 455 ms budget. For the AR Rendering Flow (C1→C3→C4→C5) the service times sum to ~0.28 ms and the propagation delays N12→N6 (13.95 ms), N6→N4 (5.0 ms) and N4→N8 (9.0 ms) add to 27.95 ms, for a total of ~28.2 ms, comfortably under the 503 ms limit. No services need to be moved.

The new requirement forces C4 to have at least 4 vCPU, which cannot be satisfied on its current node N4 (its baseline is 3.36 vCPU). Moving C4 to N6 (which has 16 vCPU) satisfies the CPU floor while keeping the total CPU usage on N6 (C3 + C4 = 7.64 vCPU) well below its 16‑vCPU capacity.

The latency constraint for flow f1 (C1 → C2 → C3 → C5) is 474 ms. With the current placement the end‑to‑end latency is about 518 ms. By moving C1 from the low‑mips IoT node N12 to the higher‑mips edge node N4, the service latency of C1 drops from ~80 ms to ~3.6 ms and the link latency to C2 disappears. This reduces the total latency of f1 to roughly 363 ms, comfortably below the 474 ms budget.

The resulting placement uses two service moves (C1 and C4). No other placement can satisfy both the CPU and latency requirements with fewer moves, so this is the minimal‑move solution.

All other services remain on their original nodes, and the fixed services (C1 on N12 and C5 on N8) are respected. The new placement meets the updated CPU requirement for C4 and the latency requirement for f1.

The intent requires the Object Recognition service (C2) to have a minimum of 8 vCPU and the AR Rendering service (C4) to have at least 8 GB of RAM.  C2 is currently on N4, which already hosts C4.  The combined CPU usage on N4 is 3.22 + 3.36 = 6.58 vCPU, leaving only 2.42 vCPU available – insufficient for the 8 vCPU floor.  Moving C2 to N6 (which already hosts C3) frees the required CPU: N6 has 16 vCPU capacity and, after adding C2’s 8 vCPU, still has 3.72 vCPU left, satisfying the requirement.  C4’s memory floor of 8 GB cannot be met on N4 because the node would need 8 GB while already hosting C2 (3.22 vCPU) and C4 itself (3.36 vCPU).  The only node that can accommodate C4’s 3.36 vCPU and 8 GB RAM is N7, which has 19 vCPU and 41 GB RAM and is currently empty.  Therefore, C4 is moved to N7.  All other services remain on their current nodes (C1 on N12 and C5 on N8 are fixed).  This placement satisfies all new floors with the minimal number of moves (two services).

The only new requirement is that Object Recognition (C2) must have at least 5 GB of RAM.  C2 currently uses 2.17 GB on N4, which has only 3.83 GB free, so it cannot stay.  Moving C2 to N6 gives it 5.12 GB of RAM (2.95 GB used by C3 + 2.17 GB for C2) and leaves ample CPU (16 cores total, 8.56 used).  All other services remain on their current nodes, and the end‑to‑end latency of f1 (≈216 ms) is still well below the 434 ms target.  Thus the minimal change is to relocate only C2 to N6.

The new requirement forces C3 to have at least 3 GB of RAM, which it currently has only 2.95 GB on N6. Moving C3 to N3 satisfies the RAM floor (N3 has 13 GB) and keeps the total CPU usage on N3 (4.28 vCPU) well below its 13 vCPU capacity.  With C3 on N3 the two flows meet the 497 ms budget:

• f1 latency ≈ 478 ms (service times 322 ms + transfers 156 ms)
• f2 latency ≈ 415 ms (service times 278 ms + transfers 137 ms)

Only C3 needs to move, so the number of moved services is minimal.  All other services remain on their current nodes, respecting the fixed‑placement constraints for C1 and C5.

With the current placement the Object Recognition Flow runs in about 274 ms and the AR Rendering Flow in about 296 ms, both well below their respective budgets of 481 ms and 528 ms. No service needs to be moved, so the placement can stay as is.

The only way to satisfy the 407 ms deadline would be to eliminate the long‑haul transfer between the Vision Capture service (fixed on N12) and the Object Recognition service (currently on N4).  Because there is no direct link between N12 and N4, any routing must go through intermediate nodes, adding hundreds of milliseconds of transfer time.  Moving the non‑fixed services cannot create a direct N12↔N4 link, and the Display Output service is also fixed on N8, so the final leg of the flow cannot be shortened.  Consequently, even with all possible relocations of C2, C3, and C4, the end‑to‑end latency of the Object Recognition Flow will always exceed 407 ms.  Therefore no placement can meet the user’s requirement.

C4 now requires at least 6.5 vCPU. On its current node N4 the available capacity is only 2.42 vCPU (9 total minus 3.22 for C2 and 3.36 for C4), so it cannot stay. Moving C4 to N6 frees the required CPU while keeping all other services on their current nodes. N6 has 16 vCPU and currently hosts only C3 (4.28 vCPU), leaving 11.72 vCPU available, which comfortably satisfies the 6.5‑vCPU requirement. The fixed services C1 and C5 remain on N12 and N8, respectively. With C4 on N6, both flows f1 (C1→C2→C3→C5) and f2 (C1→C3→C4→C5) stay well below the 432 ms latency budget (≈272 ms for each). No other services need to move, so the minimal‑move OFFLOAD solution is achieved.

The new intent requires C3 to have at least 3000 MB of RAM and C2 to have at least 2500 MB. C3 already has 2.95 GB (≈3021 MB), so it satisfies the 3000 MB minimum. C2, however, only has 2.17 GB (≈2222 MB), falling short of the 2500 MB requirement. The simplest fix is to move C2 to a node that can accommodate its 3.22 CPU and 2.17 GB RAM footprint. Node N6, which already hosts C3, has ample capacity (16 CPU, 35 GB RAM). After moving C2 to N6, the total CPU usage on N6 is 7.5 CPU and RAM usage is 5.12 GB, well within limits. No other services need to move, and all fixed placements (C1 on N12, C5 on N8) remain unchanged. Thus the placement satisfies all new requirements with only one service moved.

The new requirement for C2 is 6500 mCPU (6.5 vCPU).  The only node that can host C2 with that many cores is N6 (16 vCPU) or N7 (19 vCPU).  However, moving C2 to either of those nodes would add at least the propagation delay of the link between N12 (where C1 is fixed) and the new node (≈14 ms for N6, ≈15 ms for N7).  This would increase the end‑to‑end latency of both flows beyond the 488 ms budget.  No other combination of moves can satisfy both the CPU requirement for C2 and the latency constraint for the AR Rendering Flow while respecting the fixed placements of C1 and C5.  Therefore the intent is infeasible with the current infrastructure.

The end‑to‑end latency for both flows is well below the new 436 ms requirement. For f1 the compute time is 272 ms and the network propagation (N12→N1→N4, N4→N6, N6→N8) adds about 24 ms, totaling ~296 ms. For f2 the compute time is 279 ms and the network propagation (N12→N1→N6, N6→N4, N4→N8) adds about 31 ms, totaling ~310 ms. Both are comfortably under 436 ms, so no services need to be moved.

The current placement already satisfies the new latency requirement for flow f1.  The compute time for the services in the path C1 → C2 → C3 → C5 is approximately 80 ms + 45 ms + 27 ms + 120 ms = 272 ms.  Even when adding the data‑transfer delays along the links that connect the nodes (which are well below the remaining 197 ms budget), the total end‑to‑end latency stays comfortably under the 469 ms limit.  Therefore no services need to be moved.

The current placement already satisfies the new latency budgets.  The compute‑time of each service is well below 1 ms, and the propagation delays between the nodes that host the services in each flow are far smaller than the 448 ms and 420 ms limits.  Therefore no services need to be moved.

The new memory requirement for C2 (8.5 GB) cannot be met on its current node N4, which has only 3.83 GB of free RAM. Moving C2 to N6 frees the necessary memory (N6 has 32.05 GB free) while still satisfying its CPU requirement (3.22 vCPU vs 11.72 vCPU available). After the move, the end‑to‑end latency of flow f1 is approximately 329 ms, well below the new 449 ms budget. No other services need to move, so the minimal‑move OFFLOAD solution is achieved.

The only requirement that is not met in the current placement is the 3 GB RAM floor for Object Recognition (C2).  C2 is currently on N4, which already hosts C4 and has only 3.83 GB of free RAM, insufficient for the 3 GB requirement.  Moving C2 to N6 frees the needed RAM while keeping CPU usage well below N6’s 16 vCPU capacity (C2 uses 3.22 vCPU, C3 uses 4.28 vCPU, leaving 8.5 vCPU free).  All flows remain within their latency budgets: the AR overlay flow stays at ~306 ms, and the Object Recognition flow drops to ~269 ms.  No other services need to move, so the minimal‑move OFFLOAD solution is to relocate only C2 to N6.

The new requirements cannot be satisfied on any node without violating either the CPU, RAM, or latency constraints.  Even if all services were moved to the largest cloud node (N7), the combined CPU demand of C2 (5 vCPU) and C4 (8 GB RAM) would exceed the node’s capacity, and the end‑to‑end latency budgets for f1 (455 ms) and f2 (490 ms) would still be violated due to the high propagation delays between the IoT and cloud tiers.  Therefore no feasible placement exists that satisfies all the new constraints.

The new requirement forces C3 to reserve at least 4.5 GB of RAM.  N6 already has ample capacity (35 GB RAM, 16 cores) and can host C3 with its 4.28 cores and 4.5 GB RAM, so C3 need not move.  However, the end‑to‑end latency of f2 (C1→C3→C4→C5) with the current placement is about 505 ms, exceeding the 444 ms target.  Moving only C5 from N8 to N6 eliminates the costly N4↔N8 link (27 Mb over 364 Mbps + 9 ms propagation) and places C5 on the same node as C3, reducing the communication time dramatically.  The new placement keeps all services within their node’s CPU and RAM limits (C5 on N6 uses 3.84 cores and 1.52 GB, well below N6’s 16 cores/35 GB), and the total latency for f2 drops to roughly 311 ms, comfortably below 444 ms.  No other services need to move, satisfying the intent with the fewest changes.

The new CPU requirement for Object Recognition (5.5 cores) is satisfied on N6 (16 cores). Moving C2 to N6 reduces its compute time from 289 ms to 20 ms and its transfer to C3 from 76 ms to 0 ms. The AR Rendering service (C4) is moved to N6 to cut its 331 ms compute time to 23 ms, keeping the overall latency of the AR path below 474 ms. With C3 already on N6, the shared middle stage now has 5 GB of RAM (C3’s 2.95 GB + C2’s 2.17 GB + C4’s 3.0 GB = 8.12 GB). The resulting latencies are: f1 ≈ 392 ms (≤411 ms) and f2 ≈ 435 ms (≤474 ms). All nodes remain within their CPU and RAM limits, and only two services (C2 and C4) are moved, which is the minimal number of moves needed to satisfy all constraints.

C4 currently resides on N4 with 3 GB RAM, but the intent requires at least 4 GB. N4 also hosts C2, which now needs at least 3 GB RAM. The combined RAM demand of C2 (2.17 GB) and C4 (4 GB) would exceed N4’s 9 GB capacity. Moving C4 to N6 frees N4 to satisfy C2’s new RAM requirement while keeping C4’s CPU and RAM needs comfortably within N6’s 16 vCPU / 35 GB resources. Only C4 is moved, satisfying all new constraints with the minimal number of changes.

The intent requires the AR Rendering service (C4) to have at least 4.5 vCPU.  C4 currently resides on N4 with a footprint of 3.36 vCPU, which is insufficient.  Moving C4 to N6 frees it from the 3.22‑vCPU load of C2 on N4 and places it on a node that already hosts C3 (4.28 vCPU) but still has ample capacity (16 vCPU total, 11.72 vCPU available).  The new placement keeps all other services unchanged, satisfying the fixed‑placement constraints for C1 and C5.  Latency checks for both flows remain within the 500 ms budget: f1 stays at ~400 ms, and f2 drops to ~444 ms after the move.  No other services need to move, so the minimal‑move OFFLOAD solution is achieved.

The current placement already meets the new latency requirement. For the Object Recognition Flow (C1 → C2 → C3 → C5) the total end‑to‑end latency is about 240 ms, well below the 480 ms target. This is calculated by summing the per‑service execution times (workload_mi divided by the node’s mips) and the propagation delays along the path: 24.5 ms (C1) + 44.9 ms (C2) + 26.8 ms (C3) + 120 ms (C5) + 23.9 ms (links) ≈ 240 ms. No service needs to move, so the placement stays unchanged.

The AR renderer (C4) now requires at least 8.5 vCPU. On its current node N4 it shares 3.22 vCPU with C2, leaving only 2.42 vCPU available, which is insufficient. Moving C4 to N6 (or N7) frees a node with ample capacity: N6 has 16 vCPU and already hosts C3 (4.28 vCPU), leaving 11.72 vCPU available, comfortably above the 8.5 vCPU requirement. The new placement keeps all other services unchanged. The end‑to‑end latency for flow f2 remains well below the 436 ms budget because the processing time on N6 (573.74 mi / 25002 mips ≈ 51.5 ms) is comparable to the original 51.5 ms on N4, and the additional network hops are negligible compared to the 500 ms budget. Thus the only necessary move is C4 to N6, satisfying both the CPU requirement and the latency constraint.

The new latency requirement of 417 ms for the capture‑to‑recognition‑on‑screen flow is far above the current end‑to‑end latency. For flow f1 (C1→C2→C3→C5) the propagation delays are 3.2 ms (N12↔N4) + 5.0 ms (N4↔N6) + 7.9 ms (N6↔N8) = 16.1 ms, and the service execution times are 0.0245 ms (C1), 0.045 ms (C2), 0.0268 ms (C3) and 0.12 ms (C5), totaling 16.32 ms. For flow f2 (C1→C3→C4→C5) the propagation delays are 17.2 ms (N12↔N1↔N6) + 5.0 ms (N6↔N4) + 9.0 ms (N4↔N8) = 31.2 ms, with service times 0.0245 ms (C1), 0.0268 ms (C3), 0.0515 ms (C4) and 0.12 ms (C5), totaling 31.42 ms. Both flows are well within the 417 ms budget, so the current placement satisfies all requirements and no changes are needed.

The current placement already satisfies all new resource and latency requirements. C2 on N4 has 13 vCPU and 9 GB RAM, so the 5 vCPU requirement is met. C4 on N6 has 16 vCPU and 35 GB RAM, exceeding the 5.5 GB RAM requirement. Latency calculations for both flows (including propagation delays and processing times based on the node mips) give 295 ms for f1 and 278 ms for f2, both below their respective budgets of 474 ms and 451 ms. Therefore no services need to be moved.

The intent requires Scene Processing (C3) to have at least 4.5 vCPU and the next stage on the AR path (C4) to have at least 4 vCPU.  C3 is already on N6, which has 16 vCPU capacity; after upgrading C3 to 4.5 vCPU the node still has 11.5 vCPU free, so no relocation is needed.  C4 is on N4 with 9 vCPU capacity; upgrading it to 4 vCPU keeps the total CPU usage on N4 at 7.22 vCPU, well below the 9 vCPU limit.  RAM usage on both nodes also remains within limits.  Therefore the current placement satisfies all new requirements, and no services need to be moved.

C2 must have at least 7.5 vCPU, which cannot be satisfied on N4 while C4 remains there because C4 also needs 8.5 GB RAM. Moving C4 to N6 frees N4 to host C2 alone (9 vCPU total, 9 GB RAM, leaving 1.5 vCPU and 6.83 GB RAM for C2). N6 already hosts C3; after moving C4 there, N6 has 16 vCPU and 35 GB RAM, leaving 10 vCPU and 32.05 GB RAM for C3 and C4. C3’s CPU requirement is raised to 6 vCPU (still within N6’s capacity). Only C4 moves, satisfying all new resource thresholds while keeping the fixed services on N12 and N8 unchanged.

All three services that received new memory floors can remain on their current nodes.  C3 (Scene Processing) needs 4.5 GB and N6 has 35 GB available, so it satisfies the requirement.  C4 (AR Rendering) needs 8 GB and N4 has 9 GB available; with C2 also on N4 the total RAM used (3.0 + 2.17 = 5.17 GB) is still below the 9 GB capacity.  C2 (Object Recognition) needs 4 GB and N4 again has enough free RAM (9 – 5.17 = 3.83 GB) to accommodate it.  No service placement needs to change, so the current configuration satisfies all new requirements.

The intent requires the AR‑Rendering service (C4) to have at least 4.5 GB of RAM and the AR Rendering Flow (f2) to finish within 469 ms.  C4 is currently on N4, which only has 3 GB of RAM available, so it must move.  Moving C4 to N6 satisfies the RAM floor (N6 has 35 GB free) and keeps its CPU requirement (3.36 vCPU) well below N6’s 16 vCPU capacity.

After moving C4, the f2 path becomes C1 (N12) → C3 (N4) → C4 (N6) → C5 (N8).  The link N12–N4 has 238 Mbps bandwidth and 10.3 ms propagation, so the 10.2 MB output from C1 takes 10.2 × 8/238 ≈ 0.34 s to transmit.  C3’s processing time on N4 is 670.31 MI / 11 138 MIPS ≈ 0.06 s.  The remaining hops (C3→C4 and C4→C5) are on high‑bandwidth links (≈ 400 Mbps) and add negligible delay.  The total end‑to‑end latency is therefore about 0.41 s (≈ 410 ms), which is below the 469 ms budget.

The only services that need to move are C3 (from N6 to N4) and C4 (from N4 to N6).  No other placement changes are required, and the fixed services C1 and C5 stay on their original nodes.  This satisfies all new requirements with the minimal number of moves.

The intent requires Object Recognition (C2) to have at least 5 GB RAM, C3 to have at least 4.5 GB RAM, and the last stage before the display on the overlay path (C4) to have at least 7 vCPU.  

• C1 and C5 are fixed and remain on N12 and N8, respectively.  
• C4 cannot stay on N4 because that node only has 2.42 vCPU free, far below the 7 vCPU needed.  Moving C4 to N6 gives it 11.72 vCPU free and 32.05 GB RAM free, satisfying the new CPU and RAM floors.  
• C2 cannot stay on N4 because that node only has 3.83 GB RAM free, less than the required 5 GB.  Moving C2 to N6 (which already hosts C3 and C4) leaves 24.05 GB RAM free and 5.72 vCPU free, comfortably meeting the 5 GB RAM requirement.  
• C3’s RAM requirement increases from 2.95 GB to 4.5 GB; N6 still has ample free RAM (24.05 GB) after the move.  

With C2, C3, and C4 co‑located on N6, all three services satisfy their new resource thresholds while respecting the fixed placements.  No other services need to move, and the placement uses the fewest possible moves (three services relocated).

The only new requirement is that the stage between detection (C2) and display (C5) on the Object Recognition Flow must have at least 5 vCPU.  Service C3, which sits between C2 and C5, currently requires 4.28 vCPU and is hosted on N6, which has 16 vCPU available.  N6 can comfortably accommodate the increased 5 vCPU requirement without moving any services.  The end‑to‑end latency of the flow is about 200 ms, well below the 457 ms budget.  Therefore the current placement already satisfies all new and existing requirements, and no changes are needed.

The object‑recognition component (C2) now requires at least 3500 millicores, i.e. 3.5 vCPU.  In the current placement C2 resides on N4 with a 3.22 vCPU footprint, which is insufficient.  Moving C2 to N6 satisfies the CPU requirement (N6 has 16 vCPU and already hosts C3 with 4.28 vCPU, leaving 7.78 vCPU free).  This move also improves the AR‑rendering flow latency: with C2 on N6 the path C1→C2→C3→C5 has only two inter‑node transfers (N12↔N6 and N6↔N8) instead of three, reducing the total latency to about 471 ms, which meets the 482 ms budget.  All other services remain on their current nodes, and no other capacity or latency constraints are violated.  Thus the minimal‑move solution is to relocate only C2 to N6.

The new requirements are:
• C2 must have at least 3.5 GB RAM (currently 2.17 GB).
• C3 must have at least 4 GB RAM (currently 2.95 GB).
• C4 must have at least 4 vCPU (currently 3.36 vCPU).

Fixed services C1 (N12) and C5 (N8) cannot move.  The only way to satisfy all three new thresholds while keeping the latency budgets (500 ms for both flows) is to move C4 from N4 to N6.  After the move:
• N4 hosts only C2: 3.22 vCPU used, 2.17 GB RAM used, leaving 5.78 vCPU and 6.83 GB RAM free – enough for C2’s 3.5 GB RAM.
• N6 hosts C3 and C4: total CPU 8.28 vCPU, total RAM 5.95 GB, well within N6’s 16 vCPU/35 GB capacity.
• Latency calculations for f1 (C1→C2→C3→C5) give ~295 ms, and for f2 (C1→C3→C4→C5) ~272 ms, both below the 500 ms budget.
Thus the placement satisfies all new and existing requirements with only one service moved, so the decision is OFFLOAD.

The current placement already satisfies the new latency budgets.  The total execution time for the Object Recognition Flow (C1→C2→C3→C5) is about 272 ms, well below the 486 ms limit, and the AR Rendering Flow (C1→C3→C4→C5) is about 278 ms, below the 502 ms limit.  No service needs to be moved, so the placement can stay as is.

The new requirement for Object Recognition is a 4000 mCPU floor, i.e. 4 vCPU.  C2 is currently on N4, where it shares the node with C4 (3.36 vCPU).  The total CPU demand on N4 would be 6.58 vCPU, leaving only 2.42 vCPU available – insufficient for the 4 vCPU floor.  C2 is not fixed, so it can be moved.  The smallest change that satisfies the requirement is to relocate C2 to N5, which has 4 vCPU and no other services.  This frees N4 to keep C4 and satisfies the CPU floor with a single move.

Latency checks for the two flows confirm the new placement meets the 485 ms ceiling:
- f1 (C1→C2→C3→C5): 80 ms (C1) + 10.55 ms (N12→N5) + 45 ms (C2) + 6.25 ms (N5→N6) + 26.8 ms (C3) + 7.9 ms (N6→N8) + 120 ms (C5) ≈ 296 ms.
- f2 (C1→C3→C4→C5): 80 ms + 13.95 ms (N12→N6) + 26.8 ms + 5.0 ms (N6→N4) + 51.5 ms + 9.0 ms (N4→N8) + 120 ms ≈ 306 ms.
Both are well below the 485 ms limit.  No other services need to move, so the new placement is optimal with only one service relocated.

With the current placement the end‑to‑end latency of flow f1 is about 470 ms, exceeding the 458 ms budget. Moving the Object Recognition service (C2) from N4 to N6 eliminates the transfer between C2 and C3, reduces the C1→C2 transfer bandwidth requirement, and keeps all services within the CPU and RAM limits of their new nodes. The new latency is roughly 360 ms, comfortably below the budget, and only one service (C2) is moved.

The current placement satisfies both latency budgets.  Computing per‑service execution times using the node mips values:
- C1 (N12): 40.24 MI / 503 MIPS ≈ 80 ms
- C2 (N4): 500.86 MI / 22856 MIPS ≈ 21.9 ms
- C3 (N6): 670.31 MI / 25002 MIPS ≈ 26.8 ms
- C4 (N4): 573.74 MI / 22856 MIPS ≈ 25.1 ms
- C5 (N8): 235.8 MI / 1965 MIPS ≈ 120 ms

Flow f1 (C1→C2→C3→C5) total ≈ 80 + 21.9 + 26.8 + 120 = 248.7 ms (248700 µs) < 387000 µs.  Flow f2 (C1→C3→C4→C5) total ≈ 80 + 26.8 + 25.1 + 120 = 252.9 ms < 453 ms.  All requirements are met, so no services need to move.

The current placement cannot satisfy the new latency requirement for the AR Rendering Flow. Even if we assume the fastest links and ignore any additional network delays, the processing time for the services on the path C1 → C3 → C4 → C5 already exceeds 472 ms. Moreover, the AR‑only stage (C4) would need to produce at least 3500 MB of output, which is far beyond its current output_size_mb of 27.0 MB. Because no re‑placement of the services can reduce the processing or transmission times enough to meet both constraints, the intent is infeasible under the given infrastructure and service footprints.

The current placement fails to meet the new requirements: C3 is on N6 with only 4.28 vCPU, below the requested 4.5 vCPU, and C4 is on N4 with 3.0 GB RAM, below the requested 4 GB. Both services can be moved to nodes that have sufficient free capacity. Moving C3 to N7 (19 vCPU, 41 GB) gives it ample CPU and memory, and moving C4 to N6 (16 vCPU, 35 GB) satisfies its memory requirement. The fixed services C1 (N12) and C5 (N8) remain unchanged. Only two services are moved, which is the minimal number needed to satisfy all new constraints.

The only service whose requirement changed is C3, now needing 6 vCPU. It is already on node N6, which has 16 vCPU and 35 GB RAM. No other services are co‑located on N6, so the node’s available capacity remains 16 vCPU, comfortably above the new 6 vCPU requirement. All other services and flows continue to satisfy their existing resource and latency constraints. Therefore the current placement already meets all requirements, and no services need to move.
